body:
## Module 5 in two minutes

Every module so far has been about restraint. **This one is the highest-value AI use available to your function, it is entirely permitted, and almost nobody is doing it.**

**Disparate treatment is proven by comparators**, not by whether your investigation was careful, but by whether a similarly situated person outside the protected class was treated differently for materially the same conduct. Which means:

> **Your process quality is not the primary defence. Your consistency is.**

You can run an impeccable, well-documented investigation and lose because two years ago somebody in another unit did the same thing and got a warning. Nothing in your file is wrong. **The problem isn't in your file at all.**

And the asymmetry is the whole issue: **opposing counsel searches your case history systematically, with discovery and weeks. You ask a colleague in the ten minutes before the decision meeting**, using a memory that reconstructs the past in the direction of the decision you're about to make.

Why it's hard is measurable. **Only 32% of organizations track substantiation by issue type** — harassment, discrimination, retaliation, policy breach recorded separately rather than as one overall outcome. Without that granularity the pattern you most need is invisible: a 60% aggregate rate can hide 75% for policy breaches and 25% for harassment, and the second is the number that appears in a claim.

### Surfaces the precedent, doesn't decide it

> **AI surfaces the precedent. A human decides whether it governs.**

**Permitted, rung two:** find closed matters in this conduct category; extract per matter the conduct as recorded, the outcome, the **stated** aggravating and mitigating factors, the decision-maker, the unit, the date; flag where similar conduct produced different outcomes; list what the record cannot determine.

**Forbidden:** a recommended outcome, rung five however well it cites the precedents. Also forbidden: asking which prior matters are *closest*, because that similarity judgment is the substance of comparator analysis rather than a retrieval step.

**And the corollary that keeps the rule honest: consistency is not uniformity.** Identical conduct with different aggravating factors properly produces different outcomes. A first offence and a third are not the same case. **What the file has to contain is *why*, written by the person who decided**, the comparator analysis tells you a *why* is required; it does not supply it.

Which gives the failure mode to avoid: **an AI that flattens your case history into an average is manufacturing the disparate-treatment argument on your opponent's behalf.** Ask for "the usual outcome" and you get a central tendency; adopt it as a baseline and every legitimate difference behind the distribution has been erased into a norm you can be measured against.

**Ask for the matters and their factors. Never for the norm.** Ten rows you can check beat one sentence you cannot.

**The full module adds a distinction worth carrying into every conversation with an analytics colleague.**

**A comparator is one similarly situated individual treated differently, and a single comparator can carry a claim.** It isn't a sample, it needn't be representative, and its force doesn't depend on how many cases point the other way. **A control group is a population assembled to support an inference about an average effect**, where one case tells you nothing.

Importing intuitions between them is dangerous **in both directions**. **Dismissing a lone comparator as "n of 1" is how employers lose**. It's the statistically literate instinct and it's legally wrong. And **treating your case history as a dataset to be averaged is how employers manufacture the pattern against themselves**, because rates and disparities are the vocabulary of a different claim entirely, and once you've generated them you have to explain them.

**Then the scoping rule**, because making your case history searchable means indexing investigation notes, disciplinary records and accommodation documentation, which is the worst corpus there is for a general assistant. So: **ER team access only. Never joined to the enterprise assistant. Structured extracts over full narrative documents** — a table of conduct, outcome and factors is both safer and better at answering the question. **And raise it with counsel before you build it**, because a searchable comparator index is itself a thing that exists.

Which is the module's hardest question: **what will you do on the day the first query returns a pattern you don't like?** Settle that before you build anything.
